newsitem.title: UK: Bruised Euro currencies soothed by Iraq attack.
newsitem.headline: Bruised Euro currencies soothed by Iraq attack.

text.p: Peripheral European currencies gained some relief on Tuesday as U.S. missile attacks on Iraq boosted the dollar and oil prices, depressed the mark and deflected the market's gaze from monetary union matters.

"The currency markets are doing a typical petro-currencies trade...the relative exporters are doing well in relation to the energy importers," said Peter von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS in London.
"That explains the strength of dollar/yen, dollar/mark and sterling/mark and the softness of the Swiss franc," he added.

The French franc firmed to 3.4184 per mark before settling back at 3.4207 by 0924 GMT, little changed from its European closing level on Monday. The Italian lira strengthened to 1018.05 from late Monday's 1018.70.
The mark has grabbed hefty gains from its EU counterparts lately as the onset of the 1997 budget season stokes doubts over whether states can hammer their economies into shape for EMU.
The French franc has been especially hard hit as unions threaten to repeat last year's crippling strike action.
Now, however, tensions in the Gulf should relieve the franc slightly as the market spotlight moves, analysts said.
"There are other things going on so the focus will be able to shift from the French franc," said Deborah Read, economic adviser at BankAmerica here.
But any comfort was likely to be short-lived, analysts said. Fresh franc pain is in store when France releases second-quarter GDP data on Wednesday, expected to show the economy slowing.
The equivalent German figures, due out Thursday, should rub salt into the franc's wounds if they show the anticipated pick-up in economic growth.
Analysts noted the French currency's inability to capitalise fully on the mark's soft bias, compared to neighbours such as the Italian lira.

"Again the franc is underperforming and that's probably about right -- a lot of pressure is off for the time being but there are some big fundamental problems to be decided," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy here.
"We have cruise missiles flying around in Iraq and a lot of talk about Fed tightening, but the fundamental problems are still there for France," said Coleman.
Sterling was a notable beneficiary of the U.S. strikes on Iraq, building on gains made earlier in the week and scoring an early session high of 2.3264 marks.

"What this does mean is that within Europe you move into sterling," said Nick Parsons, forex strategist at Banque Paribas in Paris. "Sterling has never quite shaken off the petro-currency tag, even though the trade figures would give the lie to that."
Sterling/yen was especially attractive, said Parsons. "It's the most obvious petro-currency trade."

Norway, the world's second largest crude oil exporter behind Saudi Arabia, was also cited as a clear candidate for gains against the mark.The Norwegian crown rose to 4.3250 per mark from late Monday's European level of 4.3258.
But there were caveats. "The crown resists being classified as a petro-currency, though it's the purest petro-currency there is, almost on the scale of Saudi Arabia," said UBS' von Maydell.

"Norway's central bank prevents it from behaving as a petro-currency -- they try to keep it absolutely as pegged as they can keep it. It doesn't correlate very well with energy prices, even though it should in theory."
